planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing the fine seed onto the soil surface without covering since it needs light to germinate; transplant out after all frost danger has passed.

directions: Hawaii White is the pure-white counterpart to the widely grown Hawaii Blue in this classic ultra-dwarf, tight-mounding ageratum series bred for uniform bedding and edging use. It produces dense clusters of small, fuzzy, powder-puff white flowers held just above compact foliage without any pinching needed to keep plants low. Light shearing in midsummer refreshes the mound and extends bloom into fall. Pair with Hawaii Blue for a classic two-tone edging combination.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox

common_name: Sparkler Blush Cleome (Compact Spineless Spider Flower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing seed onto the surface since light aids germination; transplant after frost danger has passed, or direct sow once soil is warm.

directions: Sparkler Blush belongs to a modern breeding line developed to remove the sharp leaf-axil spines found on old-fashioned cleome types like the Queen series, making it far more pleasant to handle around beds and pathways. Flower clusters open blush white flushed with soft pink atop a naturally branching, more compact and floriferous plant than heirloom cleome. The airy, spidery blooms attract hummingbirds and pollinators all summer and hold up well as a cut flower. Deadheading spent flower heads before seed pods form keeps the plant blooming continuously into fall.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox

common_name: Sparkler Lavender Cleome (Compact Spineless Spider Flower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing seed onto the surface since light aids germination; transplant after frost danger has passed, or direct sow once soil is warm.

directions: Sparkler Lavender shares the compact, spineless habit of the Sparkler breeding line but carries soft violet-lavender flowers in large, airy, spidery clusters atop strong branching stems. Its shorter, tidier stature compared to heirloom Queen-series cleome suits large containers and mixed borders where taller old-fashioned types would flop or need staking. Plants bloom non-stop through summer heat and humidity, drawing hummingbirds and butterflies, and hold well when cut for arrangements. Removing developing seed pods regularly encourages continued flowering rather than a shift to seed production.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox

common_name: Nicki Red Flowering Tobacco (Compact Day-Blooming Nicotiana)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, surface-sowing without covering since seed needs light to germinate; transplant after all frost danger has passed.

directions: Nicki Red is part of the long-established Nicki series, one of the first flowering-tobacco strains bred to hold its trumpet-shaped blooms open through the day rather than closing in bright sun as many older nicotiana types do. Rich velvety-red flowers cover a compact, uniform mound well suited to bedding and container use, in contrast to the much taller, floppier species forms. Evening and early-morning fragrance remains strong even though the flowers stay open all day. Deadheading spent blooms keeps plants tidy and encourages continued flowering through the season.

common_name: Nicki White Flowering Tobacco (Compact Day-Blooming Nicotiana)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, surface-sowing without covering since seed needs light to germinate; transplant after all frost danger has passed.

directions: Nicki White carries pure white, star-throated trumpet flowers on the same compact, uniform Nicki-series plants bred to stay open through the day instead of closing in sunlight, a trait that set this series apart from older flowering tobaccos when it was introduced. The clean white color glows in evening gardens and pairs easily with almost any bedding scheme. Plants are noticeably shorter and more floriferous than species Nicotiana alata, making them well suited to borders and large containers. Fragrance is strongest in early morning and evening, drawing sphinx moths and other pollinators.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown starts after all danger of frost has passed, in rich, well-drained soil; where not hardy, lift and store tubers over winter like dahlias or grow as a container plant brought indoors.

directions: Chocamocha is a patented, sterile hybrid selection of chocolate cosmos bred for heavier, more continuous bloom than the true species, which is now nearly extinct in the wild and can only be propagated vegetatively. Because it sets no seed, all of the plant's energy goes into producing deep maroon-brown, chocolate-scented flowers over a long summer season rather than into seed production. It is more vigorous and heat-tolerant than straight Cosmos atrosanguineus, though it still benefits from winter protection or lifting outside its hardiness range. The rich fragrance is strongest on warm afternoons, making it a favorite near patios and walkways.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox

common_name: Double Click Mother of Pearl Cosmos (Double-Flowered Cut Flower)
scientific_name: Cosmos bipinnatus 'Double Click Mother of Pearl'

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed in average, well-drained soil, or start indoors 3-4 weeks earlier for a head start; thin seedlings once established.

directions: Double Click Mother of Pearl produces fully double to semi-double blush-white and pale pink ruffled blooms that resemble small dahlias, part of the Double Click strain bred for a high percentage of double-flowered plants from seed rather than the single daisy form typical of most cosmos. Tall, airy, wiry stems make it an excellent cut flower that holds up well in arrangements, and frequent cutting or deadheading keeps plants blooming over a long summer season. Like other cosmos, it thrives in lean, well-drained soil and average water, flowering poorly and flopping if the soil is too rich. Bees and other pollinators visit the blooms freely even though the extra petals are a departure from the wild single form.

common_name: Early Splendor Amaranth (Joseph's Coat Foliage Annual)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, or start indoors 4-6 weeks earlier; thin seedlings to final spacing since plants dislike root disturbance.

directions: Early Splendor is a classic Joseph's coat type grown for its dramatic foliage rather than its inconspicuous flowers, with dark bronze-purple-red lower leaves topped by a brilliant crimson-scarlet cap of color at the crown of each strongly branching plant. It was recognized decades ago as an outstanding garden performer and remains a reliable, compact choice for hot, sunny beds and large containers where its color intensifies rather than fades in summer heat. Plants tolerate poor, dry soil far better than most bedding annuals and need little supplemental feeding. Pinching young plants encourages a bushier, more colorful habit.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox

common_name: Gnome Purple Globe Amaranth (Dwarf Everlasting Bedding Gomphrena)

planting.note: Soak seed overnight and start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, since gomphrena germinates slowly; transplant out only after soil and air have warmed well past last frost.

directions: Gnome Purple is the violet-purple companion to the widely grown Gnome Pink, part of an old dwarf compact globe amaranth strain that stays just 6-9 inches tall for edging, rock gardens, and small containers where taller gomphrena would be out of scale. The rounded, clover-like flower heads are made of papery bracts that hold their rich purple color for months when cut and air-dried, making this miniature form as valuable for everlasting arrangements as it is in the garden. Plants shrug off the heat, humidity, and drought that stress most other summer bedding annuals, and need little more than lean, well-drained soil and full sun. Established plants flower continuously from early summer through frost with minimal deadheading required.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox
